system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2194-09-05 19:40:00 to 2194-09-07 19:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, a functioning pancreatic transplant, mechanical mitral valve on anticoagulation, and systolic heart failure was admitted for fever, nausea, and vomiting. She was transferred from an outside hospital where she received antibiotics and imaging showed gallbladder wall thickening and stranding around a failed renal graft. Evaluation revealed no acute cholecystitis on ultrasound and no source of bacterial infection; blood cultures were negative. Her symptoms resolved, and liver enzymes normalized, consistent with a viral syndrome. Her INR was supratherapeutic at 6.6, peaking at 10, prompting administration of vitamin K. INR stabilized at 2.9, and warfarin was restarted at 5 mg daily. She underwent one session of hemodialysis, which improved her renal function and overall stability. She was discharged home with instructions to monitor INR, resume her regular dialysis schedule, and follow up with her primary care and transplant teams.
problems: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Ulcer of other part of foot

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having a lot of pain in my left leg. It started after I got bitten at dialysis last week. I kept scratching it because it was itchy, but then it got hard and really sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when did the pain and fever start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two days ago. I woke up with chills, couldn’t get out of bed, and my leg felt hot. I was nauseous and threw up a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. At the outside hospital, they started you on antibiotics—vancomycin, levaquin, and clindamycin—because they saw signs of cellulitis, which is a skin infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they said it might be from the bug bite. But I didn’t see anything there—no pus or open wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. The ultrasound didn’t show a clot or abscess, so we’re treating it as nonpurulent cellulitis. We’ll continue vancomycin since you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about MRSA? I’ve been in the hospital a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was a concern, but since there’s no pus, staph infection is less likely. We’ve stopped levaquin and clindamycin and will stick with vancomycin for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my other meds? I usually take 5 mg of warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR came back at 4, which is high. That means your blood is too thin. You were only taking 4 mg of warfarin recently—was that a change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my nurse suggested 4 mg last week. I didn’t know it could cause problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially with antibiotics. We’ve held warfarin for now. Once your INR is safer, we’ll restart it at 5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my heart valve? I’m on it because of the mechanical mitral valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re monitoring closely. The risk is low over a couple of days, especially since you’re not moving much. We’ll restart soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel better knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. White count is still a bit low but not concerning. The infection seems to be responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My leg does feel less tender today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep the vancomycin going. Also, your kidney function is expected to worsen with infection. Creatinine went up to 7.5, but that’s common in this situation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m supposed to have dialysis tomorrow. Will that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re scheduled for hemodialysis tomorrow morning. It’ll help clear toxins and improve how you feel overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my INR? Any update?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s coming down. We’ll check again tomorrow. If it’s below 3, we’ll restart warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like tacrolimus and prednisone for my transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still taking those twice daily. We’re watching for any drug interactions, but so far, everything looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I took tramadol earlier, but I might not need it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Also, we’re restarting metoprolol today. It was held because of low blood pressure, but you’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take that for my heart. Is it safe with the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it helps your heart function. We’ll monitor your blood pressure and heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. Your INR is now 2.8—safe to restart warfarin. We’ll give you 5 mg today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue it at home through your dialysis sessions for a full 10-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll get it during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The dialysis team will give you 500 mg each session until it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today, once you finish dialysis. You’re doing well—alert, walking, no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to check my INR again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your first check should be tomorrow. Keep taking warfarin daily, and report any unusual bruising or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my foot ulcer—I changed the dressing yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the bactroban and santyl as before. The vascular team will follow up on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Call us if you develop fever, worsening pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis and all set. Your labs are stable, leg is improving, and you’re back on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Remember to weigh yourself daily and call if you gain more than 3 pounds. Follow up with your primary doctor and transplant team.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including end-stage renal disease, pancreatic transplant, mechanical mitral valve, and heart failure was admitted for left leg cellulitis following a bug bite at her dialysis center. She presented with fever, chills, nausea, and worsening leg pain. She had been on reduced-dose warfarin, leading to an elevated INR of 4 on admission. She was treated with intravenous vancomycin after initial broad-spectrum antibiotics at an outside hospital. Her infection improved, INR normalized, and warfarin was safely restarted. She received one session of hemodialysis during admission and was transitioned back to her baseline medications, including metoprolol, which had been held. She was discharged home with a plan to complete a 10-day course of vancomycin via dialysis, monitor INR, and follow up with her care teams.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Anticoagulants causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Heart valve replaced by other means
Ulcer of other part of foot
